## Statement

Trial eligibility is assessed at a screening visit; a database records what a clinician happened to order. Restricting an emulation to patients with complete eligibility information therefore selects on laboratory testing, clinical documentation and specialist access, which differ systematically from the excluded patients. Weighting methods for missing eligibility have recently been developed and the literature remains small. The harder version of the problem is that eligibility is latent rather than merely missing: an absent creatinine value is consistent both with a patient who would have failed the criterion and with one who was never tested, and the missingness itself may depend on treatment anticipation or on the impending outcome.

## Why it is open

Missing-at-random conditional on the recorded history is not credible here, because the recording decision is a clinical judgment informed by exactly the severity that predicts the outcome. Distinguishing latent eligibility from missing measurement requires a validation source in which the criterion was assessed for everyone, and such sources are rare and rarely representative. Imputing the value and imputing eligibility are different operations with different targets, and the literature has not separated them.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Benz L, et al. Adjusting for selection bias due to missing eligibility criteria in emulated target trials. Am J Epidemiol 2025](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwae471) | Develops weighting for missing eligibility information in emulated trials, the first direct treatment of the problem. |
| [Wang, et al. An operational target trial emulation framework for causal inference using electronic health records. npj Digit Med 2026](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-026-02563-z) | Sets out how each protocol component, eligibility included, is realized against record-level data and where the realization is partial. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Model true eligibility and its observation jointly, using validation records where a criterion was assessed for everyone to anchor the measurement model. Compare multiple imputation, inverse-probability-of-eligibility weighting, doubly robust selection correction and partial-identification bounds on the same data, since they make different assumptions and currently no one knows which are tolerable. Report the eligible population under each approach alongside the effect estimate, because a method that changes who is in the trial has changed the estimand and should be read that way.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.

**Dissent.** literature dissented (open): The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. [...]

4 of the 4 independent auditors returned an opinion on this entry.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **open / supported-with-caveat.** The entry says the literature on missing eligibility is small. It is small and it is larger than the one paper the entry cites. A 2026 Statistics in Medicine paper treats missingness in eligibility criteria for target trial emulation in electronic health records with survival outcomes, alongside the 2025 American Journal of Epidemiology weighting paper the entry already carries. The harder claim, that eligibility is latent rather than missing and that an absent value is consistent with both a failed criterion and an untested patient, is not addressed by either and stands.
    Cites 10.1002/sim.70500: A second and more recent direct treatment of the problem, which the entry's claim of a very small literature should acknowledge..
    Cites 10.1093/aje/kwae471: The weighting approach the entry already cites..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **partially-solved / overstated.** Restricting analysis to records with observed eligibility can cause selection bias, but systematic differences between included and excluded patients do not alone establish bias for a specified causal estimand. Identification depends on conditional exchangeability for the observation or selection process and adequate observed support. When true eligibility is missing not at random, the effect among truly eligible patients is generally not identified from the main data alone. However, assessing the criterion for everyone in a validation source is sufficient, not necessary. A probability validation subsample, auxiliary-variable restrictions, explicit parametric assumptions, sensitivity analysis, or partial-identification methods can also inform the problem. If eligibility is a deterministic threshold of an underlying measurement, imputing that measurement and deriving eligibility can target the same population as directly imputing eligibility. Changing imputed membership across draws represents missing-data uncertainty and does not automatically change the estimand. Existing weighting work addresses an important identified-assumption case, while the unrestricted latent-eligibility problem remains open.
    Cites doi:10.1093/aje/kwae471: Provides a weighting approach for selection arising from missing eligibility information under identifying assumptions; it does not nonparametrically identify unrestricted missing-not-at-random latent eligibility..

Grok 4.5, recency lens
:   **partially-solved / supported-with-caveat.** Inverted prior: treat missing-eligibility selection as already handled, then check what exists. Three direct method papers (not one) address the complete-case selection problem under explicit missingness models. Tompsett et al. (2023) formalize bias from missing eligibility in a point-treatment TTE, show patterns under MAR and MNAR, and evaluate multiple imputation of the eligibility-defining variables plus MNAR sensitivity shifts; they state that MNAR imputation remains exploratory because the sensitivity parameters are not identified from the data alone. Benz et al. (2025; also arXiv:2406.16830), which the entry cites as the first direct treatment, develops inverse-probability-of-ascertainment weights for sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption (ascertainment independent of true eligibility given non-eligibility covariates and treatment), evaluates them in plasmode EHR simulations, and applies them to a Kaiser Permanente bariatric-surgery cohort; accompanying research code is on GitHub (lbenz730/missing_eligibility_tte), not a production CRAN/Python package. Shen et al. (2026, Stat Med) compares complete-case analysis with three multiple-imputation strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs and reports that flexible MI often reduces bias when missingness is high. Wang et al. (2026) map eligibility realization in EHR data and cite Tompsett and Benz as the handling literature; they do not add a new estimator. What remains open, and matches the entry’s harder claim, is latent eligibility: an absent lab is consistent with never-tested versus would-have-failed, with recording driven by the same severity that predicts treatment and outcome (MNAR not cured by MAR IPW or standard MI). No paper retrieved jointly models true eligibility and its observation process anchored to a validation source where the criterion was assessed for everyone; no head-to-head of MI, IPW, doubly robust selection correction, and partial-identification bounds on the same TTE data with reporting of the implied eligible population under each method was found. Package search (TrialEmulation, WeightIt missing-covariate handling, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, zEpid, causallib) shows no shipped inverse-probability-of-eligibility-ascertainment or joint latent-eligibility measurement model. 2025–2026 guidance (TARGET, FDA RWE/ECT, EMA registry, NICE RWE) does not resolve identification of latent eligibility. Partial solve covers MAR complete-case selection; the title problem (unrecorded criterion indistinguishable from met criterion) stays open.
    Cites 10.1093/aje/kwac202: Partial: identifies and simulates selection bias from missing eligibility in TTE; evaluates MI of eligibility-defining variables and MNAR sensitivity imputation for recovering the eligible-population ACE under stated MAR/MNAR mechanisms (point treatment, continuous/binary outcome setting)..
    Cites 10.1093/aje/kwae471: Partial: IPW framework for selection due to incomplete eligibility ascertainment in sequential TTE with time-to-event endpoints under an eligibility-MAR assumption; simulation evaluation and real EHR application. Does not identify effects when missingness depends on latent eligibility itself..
    Cites 10.1002/sim.70500: Partial: compares complete-case analysis versus three MI strategies for eligibility-defining variables in EHR survival TTEs; empirical guidance on when flexible MI reduces bias under high missingness. Still imputes recorded values rather than separating latent eligibility from observation..
    Cites arxiv:2406.16830: Same as Benz 2025 AJE; states the eligibility-MAR assumption used by the weights and makes clear that standard complete-case analysis targets a different estimand (eligible complete cases, not all eligible)..

GLM-5.2, third independent lens
:   **open / supported.** The claim is internally consistent and pitched at the right level of generality. It correctly identifies that restricting to complete cases selects on healthcare utilization, and that the latent eligibility problem is distinct from simple missingness. The stated reasons for the problem being open (MAR is not credible, validation sources are rare, and imputing a value is different from imputing eligibility) logically entail that the problem remains open. The claim does not assert an impossibility but rather a current methodological gap and a structural difficulty in distinguishing latent states from missing measurements.

Decision path
:   `R3:partially-solved(n=2/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex`

:::

## How the evidence falls in time

47 papers in the reviewed corpus bear on this problem, published 2016 to 2026. Partial progress is on the record, and later work still calls this open. Both belong in view.

This problem is **recurrent**: three or more papers spanning at least eight years assert it independently. Sustained restatement by authors who mostly do not cite each other is the strongest evidence this reading can offer that a gap is real rather than one group's framing.

It is also being **closed in pieces**: partial results come from more than one paper in more than one year, each covering a different part.
